facts.claim: "Demons" is the opening track (4:11) on Jacob Lee's album Philosophy, released February 1, 2019.
Jacob Lee is credited as songwriter, composer and lyricist of "Demons", and Matt Bartlem as producer.
Philosophy is Lee's debut studio album. It came out on his independent label, Philosophical Records, and he also owns the Lowly Lyricist brand.
Sputnikmusic describes "Demons" as staying mostly within pop-rock. Its bridge has a guitar solo surrounded by swelling synthesisers. The review says the song opens the album with a punch.
In a track-by-track piece, Lee recalls the adrenaline he felt while writing "Demons". He says it returned later, after about four months of doubt, when he felt he might be writing something decent.
Lee says every track of his was written alone, behind closed doors, on an acoustic guitar. The band-style production was added afterward.
Lee grew up on the Gold Coast, Australia. He watched his father rehearse for shows, and his father gave him his first guitar and taught him the basics of chords and songwriting.
Lee began posting individual tracks online in 2014. When asked about songwriting influences, he named only prose authors: Marcus Aurelius, Paulo Coelho and Mitch Albom.

Before Philosophy, Lee released the EPs Sine Qua Non (2016) and Clarity (2017). "Demons" was also issued as a standalone single in 2017, and a re-recorded "Philosophical Sessions" version appeared in 2019.
Lee's second album is titled Conscience. He described his songwriting as obsessed with philosophy and lyricism.

research.lineage: Jacob Lee is an Australian (Gold Coast) independent alternative-pop singer-songwriter. His songs are acoustic-guitar-written and lyric-driven, with pop-rock and electronic production.

draft:
"Deep in my structure, I think I still love her." *Structure* is a strange word for a love song. It's more blueprint than heartbeat, and it shows how the narrator of **Demons** sees himself: as something built and load-bearing, now cracking. Later he names a rupture where she should be. Jacob Lee writes like someone trying to reason through a feeling that won't be reasoned with. That fits a songwriter who, asked about influences, named Marcus Aurelius, Paulo Coelho and Mitch Albom rather than any musician.

The betrayal here is specific. The "you" didn't just leave. They switched sides. "But you took their side and you pulled them to freedom" is the chorus's sharp turn. He had been doing the slow work of keeping his worst self locked down, and someone he trusted opened the door. Then comes the line that carries the hurt: "I kept your secrets and I thought that you would do the same." It's a ledger, a fairness argument, and the self-justification sits right next to the wound. He needs it on record that he held up his end. Notice that "her" is spoken about while "you" is spoken to. The song never says whether they're the same person, so grief and accusation stay tangled. Even his requests are small and worn out: sleep, breath, peace.

Lee says he writes everything alone, behind closed doors, on an acoustic guitar, with the band arrangement added afterward. Here that came from producer Matt Bartlem. A driving mid-tempo beat, kick and snare hitting square, runs under a sustained synth pad while a distorted electric guitar chugs. Lee's voice is clear and a little breathy, and stacked harmonies thicken the lead. In quieter stretches the drums ease back, a clean arpeggiated guitar comes forward, and the vocal turns close and intimate. Sputnikmusic heard it as mostly pop-rock, with a bridge guitar solo wrapped in swelling synths, and called it a punchy opener for *Philosophy*, his debut.

Lee clearly knew it mattered. He recalls the adrenaline of writing it coming back after about four months of doubt, the sense that he might finally be making something decent. He released it as a single in 2017, re-recorded it, then put it first on the album. Late in the song the chorus repeats so many times it stops sounding like a complaint and starts sounding like someone saying it over until it makes sense.

What sticks is that last line's quiet bookkeeping, the way you keep counting the secrets you kept when the loyalty never came back.
